title: Data classes, equality, enums, objects
scopeHtml: Scope: data class generated members, copy/destructuring, == vs === and the equals/hashCode contract, enum classes (entries, when, EnumMap), object declarations, companion objects, data object (Kotlin 1.9+).

questions.promptHtml: What does the compiler generate for a data class, and which properties take part in it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the most common Kotlin warm-up question, and a quick way to find out who knows the "primary constructor only" rule and who just says "it generates getters".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For a data class the compiler generates equals(), hashCode(), toString(), copy() and component1()..componentN(). All of them use only the properties declared in the primary constructor. A property declared in the class body is invisible to every generated member. If I write equals, hashCode or toString myself, or a supertype has a final version, the compiler doesn't generate that member. copy and componentN can't be hand-written.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A data class is an ordinary final JVM class plus generated members. The requirements are:

  • The primary constructor has at least one parameter, and every parameter is val or var.
  • The class can't be abstract, open, sealed or inner.
  • It can extend a class and implement interfaces (allowed since Kotlin 1.1).

Here is what you get for data class User(val id: Long, val name: String?), roughly as decompiled:

Member Generated behavior
toString() "User(id=1, name=Ann)": class name plus primary-ctor props in declaration order
hashCode() result = id.hashCode(); result = 31 * result + (name?.hashCode() ?: 0)
equals(other) this === other → true; other !is User → false; then compares each prop (Intrinsics.areEqual for references, Long/Int compared directly, Float/Double via compare)
copy(id = this.id, name = this.name) new instance; default args are the current values
component1(), component2() return id, name in order, for destructuring

Two runtime details a senior candidate should know:

  1. The generated equals short-circuits on identity (===) first. If both sides are the same instance, the comparison costs O(1).
  2. For Double/Float properties the generated equals compares with java.lang.Double.compare-style total ordering. Two Point(Double.NaN) instances are therefore equal, while Point(0.0) != Point(-0.0). That differs from 0.0 == -0.0 on primitives. Confirm this with Kotlin Bytecode → Decompile for your compiler version.

The generated members aren't cached. hashCode() is recomputed on every call, and it walks nested lists and maps fully.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class User(val id: Long, val name: String) {
    var lastSeen: Long = 0L // body property: NOT in equals/hashCode/toString/copy
}

fun main() {
    val a = User(1, "Ann").apply { lastSeen = 100 }
    val b = User(1, "Ann").apply { lastSeen = 999 }
    println(a == b)            // true: lastSeen ignored
    println(a)                 // User(id=1, name=Ann): no lastSeen
    println(a.copy().lastSeen) // 0: copy() only passes ctor params
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming body properties take part in equality. They are silently ignored, including by copy(), so the value is reset to its initializer.
  • Assuming you can override copy() or componentN() by hand. Explicit implementations are compile errors.
  • Putting Array properties in a data class: equality on them is by reference. See Q049.
  • Treating toString() as safe to log. It prints every primary property, including tokens and PII.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do I exclude a field from equality? → Move it to the class body, or override equals/hashCode by hand. The body approach also excludes it from copy, which may be a bug.
  2. Can a data class have no properties? → No, it needs at least one ctor parameter. Use data object for the stateless case (Q047).
  3. What happens if a superclass declares final override fun toString()? → The data class inherits it and the compiler doesn't generate one. The same applies to equals and hashCode.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists the five members. The senior answer adds the primary-constructor-only rule and its consequences for copy(), the identity short-circuit, the Double total-order semantics, the fact that hashCode is uncached, and the PII risk of the generated toString.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A login data class Session(val user: String, val token: String) ended up in Crashlytics logs through string templates. The fix was overriding toString() to redact the token.

questions.promptHtml: What's the difference between == and === in Kotlin, and what does a == b compile to?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks the Java-to-Kotlin mental model shift, and whether you know how nulls and floating point behave under each operator.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: == is structural equality. It compiles to a?.equals(b) ?: (b === null), so it's null-safe and calls equals. === is referential equality: same object or not, and it never calls equals. One trap: for Float/Double statically typed as such, == follows IEEE 754 (NaN != NaN, 0.0 == -0.0). When the static type is Any or generic, == falls back to equals(), which has the opposite results.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
a == b    ->  if (a == null) b == null else a.equals(b)   // Intrinsics.areEqual(a, b)
a != b    ->  !(a == b)
a === b   ->  reference comparison (JVM if_acmpeq), no method call
  • equals can't be overloaded as an operator. You override open operator fun equals(other: Any?): Boolean from Any.
  • x == null compiles to a plain null check, so it has no cost.
  • For primitive-typed values (Int, Long) == compares values directly. === on them is deprecated (warning "Identity equality for arguments of types Int and Int is deprecated") because the result depends on boxing. The Integer cache trap is covered in chunk K1b.
  • Floating point depends on the static type:
Static type NaN == NaN 0.0 == -0.0
Double / Double? false (IEEE 754) true
Any, Comparable<Double>, T true (Double.equals) false

This matters in generic code. A List<Double>.contains(Double.NaN) returns true, while Double.NaN == Double.NaN returns false.

  • For data object and enums, == and === give the same result in normal code. Docs still advise == for data objects because reflection or serialization can create a second instance (Q047).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val a = "hello"
val b = StringBuilder("hel").append("lo").toString()
println(a == b)   // true  - equals()
println(a === b)  // false - different String objects

val x: Double = Double.NaN
val y: Any = Double.NaN
println(x == x)        // false - IEEE
println(y == y)        // true  - Double.equals
println(listOf(x).contains(Double.NaN)) // true - uses equals

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using === on strings because "it worked in tests". Literals are interned, but runtime-built strings aren't.
  • Expecting == on two Arrays to compare contents. It compares references, so use contentEquals.
  • Forgetting that == on a type whose equals is broken inherits the bug. == is only as good as equals.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a == b safe if a is null? → Yes, it compiles to a null check before calling equals.
  2. When would you deliberately use ===? → Identity checks: "did this list instance change" shortcuts, sentinels, DiffUtil.areItemsTheSame on stable cached instances. Never for value comparison.
  3. Why does setOf(0.0).contains(-0.0) return false? → Set uses Double.equals/hashCode, which separates 0.0 and -0.0, while 0.0 == -0.0 on primitives is true.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "== is equals, === is reference". The senior answer adds the exact null-safe expansion, the static-type dependency for floating point, the identity deprecation for primitives, and when identity checks are a legitimate optimization.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A price-dedupe step keyed Map<Any, ...> by boxed Double treated -0.0 and 0.0 as different keys, and users saw two "free" rows. The fix was normalizing to BigDecimal/cents.

questions.promptHtml: State the equals/hashCode contract. What goes wrong in a HashMap if I override equals but not hashCode, and how does inheritance break equals?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Glassdoor senior lists literally include "What can go wrong with equals() and hashCode()?". It separates people who've debugged a hash collection from people who memorized a definition.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent and return false for null. Equal objects must have equal hash codes, though unequal objects may collide. If I override equals without hashCode, two equal objects land in different buckets, so map[key] misses and a Set holds duplicates. With inheritance, an is-based equals in a base class plus an extra field in a subclass breaks symmetry. That's why data classes are final and compare with other !is Type.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
How HashMap.get(k) works:

h = spread(k.hashCode())            // 1. pick bucket by hash
bucket = table[h & (n-1)]
for node in bucket:                 // 2. within bucket:
    if node.hash == h && (node.key === k || node.key.equals(k)) return node.value

The hash picks the bucket first, so equals only ever runs between keys whose hashes match. Here's what each kind of violation does:

Violation Symptom
equals overridden, hashCode not (identity hash) map[User(1)] returns null for an equal key; Set dedupe fails
hashCode uses a mutable field, mutated after insert entry becomes unreachable ("lost" key), memory leak in caches
equals asymmetric (a == b but b != a) list.contains result depends on argument order; distinct() nondeterministic
hashCode constant (e.g. = 1) still correct, but every key lands in one bucket. Java 8+ treeifies a bucket at 8 entries (once table capacity ≥ 64); lookups are roughly O(log n) only if keys are Comparable, otherwise they degrade toward O(n)

The inheritance problem:

open class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int) {
    override fun equals(other: Any?) = other is Point && x == other.x && y == other.y
    override fun hashCode() = 31 * x + y
}
class ColorPoint(x: Int, y: Int, val color: Int) : Point(x, y) {
    override fun equals(other: Any?) =
        other is ColorPoint && super.equals(other) && color == other.color
}
// Point(1,2) == ColorPoint(1,2,RED)  -> true
// ColorPoint(1,2,RED) == Point(1,2)  -> false  (symmetry broken)

There are three ways out:

  • Make the class final, as data classes are.
  • Compare javaClass == other.javaClass. This keeps symmetry but violates Liskov, since a subclass is never equal to its parent.
  • Use composition instead of inheritance.

Floating-point fields: use compare/toBits semantics, as the generated data class code does (Q036).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Key(val id: Int) {
    override fun equals(other: Any?) = other is Key && other.id == id
    // BUG: no hashCode override -> identity hash
}

fun main() {
    val m = hashMapOf(Key(1) to "a")
    println(m[Key(1)])   // null (almost always): different bucket
}

// Correct, manual version for a non-data class:
class GoodKey(val id: Int, val tag: String) {
    override fun equals(other: Any?): Boolean {
        if (this === other) return true
        if (other !is GoodKey) return false
        return id == other.id && tag == other.tag
    }
    override fun hashCode(): Int = 31 * id + tag.hashCode()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing fun equals(other: Key), an overload instead of an override. Kotlin requires override with Any?, which catches this, but Java code doesn't.
  • Including lazily computed or mutable fields in hashCode.
  • Making equals depend on something like Context or time.
  • Relying on "the test passed". With an identity hash, a lookup occasionally hits by chance when both keys end up in the same bucket.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can two unequal objects have the same hash? → Yes, that's a collision. It's legal, it just costs performance.
  2. Why 31 in hashCode? → It's an odd prime, and 31 * i == (i << 5) - i is cheap. It's a convention, not a correctness requirement.
  3. How does a data class avoid the symmetry problem? → It's final, and its equals checks other !is Self. If you extend an open base with its own equals, you can still create asymmetry, so keep the base's equals abstract or final.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer recites "override both". The senior answer explains bucket lookup mechanics, why mutable fields in hash codes lose entries, the subclass symmetry break, and the javaClass vs is trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An image cache keyed by a hand-written RequestKey that lacked hashCode had a 0% hit rate. Memory looked like a leak and network was 3x the expected volume. The one-line fix was converting it to a data class.

questions.promptHtml: Is a data class copy() deep or shallow? What are the consequences, and what changed about copy() visibility in Kotlin 2.x?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Immutable UI state is built on copy(). Shallow-copy bugs show up as "UI not updating" and "state mutated from somewhere else".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: copy() is shallow. It calls the primary constructor with the same references for every property I don't override, so a MutableList or nested mutable object is shared between the original and the copy. That's fine and fast if everything nested is immutable, and dangerous if anything is mutable. On visibility: before Kotlin 2.0.20, copy() was always public, even with a private constructor, which let callers bypass validation. 2.0.20 started a deprecation cycle so that copy matches the constructor's visibility. You opt in now with @ConsistentCopyVisibility or -Xconsistent-data-class-copy-visibility.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
val a = State(items = mutableListOf(1,2), user = User("x"))
val b = a.copy(loading = true)

a ──► State ─┬─ items ──► [ArrayList 1,2] ◄──┐
             └─ user  ──► User("x")  ◄──┐   │
b ──► State ─┬─ items ──────────────────┼───┘   (same list)
             └─ user  ──────────────────┘       (same User)
  • Cost: copy() is one allocation plus field copies, and doesn't recurse. That's why immutable-state architectures are cheap.
  • Danger: b.items.add(3) also changes a. Anything comparing old to new, such as DiffUtil, StateFlow's distinct check or Compose skipping, now sees "old == new" because both point at the mutated list.
  • Deep copy isn't provided. You copy nested parts explicitly: copy(items = items.toList()), write per-type copy functions, or better, make nested types immutable (List, kotlinx.collections.immutable per chunk K7) so sharing is safe.
  • Body properties aren't passed to copy() (Q036), so their initializer values come back.
  • The copy() visibility change (verify the exact version for your toolchain against KT-11914):
    • 2.0.20 added warnings when a data class with a non-public constructor exposes copy.
    • Later 2.x releases escalate this to an error, then flip the default.
    • @ConsistentCopyVisibility opts in early: copy gets the constructor's visibility.
    • @ExposedCopyVisibility keeps the old public binary signature during migration.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Validated value via private constructor
@ConsistentCopyVisibility // Kotlin 2.0.20+: copy() becomes private like the ctor
data class Email private constructor(val value: String) {
    companion object {
        fun of(raw: String): Email? =
            raw.trim().takeIf { "@" in it }?.let(::Email)
    }
}
// Without the annotation (pre-change default), callers could do:
// Email.of("a@b.c")!!.copy(value = "not-an-email")  // validation bypassed

// Shallow copy trap
data class Cart(val items: MutableList<String>)
fun main() {
    val a = Cart(mutableListOf("apple"))
    val b = a.copy()
    b.items += "pear"
    println(a.items) // [apple, pear]
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using copy() as a "clone" before mutating nested state.
  • Declaring val items: MutableList<T> in UI state. val only freezes the reference, not the contents.
  • Assuming a private constructor is enough for invariants on pre-2.x behavior when copy is public.
  • Running heavy validation in init and forgetting that copy() also runs init. It does, because it calls the constructor, so that's actually good for invariants but costs CPU in hot copy loops.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does copy() run init blocks? → Yes, it's a constructor call.
  2. How would you deep-copy a graph-shaped state? → Usually you don't. You make it immutable and structurally share it. If you really must, write explicit mapping or serialize/deserialize, which is slow.
  3. Why not make copy() deep by default? → Cost would become proportional to graph size, cycles would recurse forever, and identity-based shortcuts like === in equals and DiffUtil identity checks would be lost. Structural sharing is the point.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "shallow, so nested objects are shared". The senior answer adds the aliasing consequences for diffing and state flows, the immutability-instead-of-deep-copy design choice, copy running init, and the 2.0.20+ copy visibility migration with its annotations.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A UiState(filters: MutableSet<Filter>) was "copied", then mutated, then emitted. StateFlow saw an equal value and dropped it, so the filter chip toggled only visually on the next unrelated emission.

questions.promptHtml: How does destructuring like val (id, name) = user work, and what's the risk of using it on data classes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you know destructuring is positional sugar over componentN(), and whether you've seen the refactoring hazard.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Destructuring compiles to calls to component1(), component2() and so on. Those are operator functions that a data class generates in primary-constructor order. Any class can opt in by declaring operator fun componentN(). The risk is that it's positional, not by name. If someone reorders two same-typed properties in the constructor, every destructuring site silently swaps values and still compiles.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• val (a, b) = x compiles to val a = x.component1(); val b = x.component2().
  • Where it's used:
    • Lambdas: map.forEach { (k, v) -> }. Note that { (k, v) -> } is one destructured param, while { k, v -> } is two params.
    • for ((i, v) in list.withIndex()).
    • Pair and Triple.
    • Map.Entry, through stdlib extension component1/2.
  • Use _ to skip: val (_, name) = user. The compiler doesn't call component1() for _.
  • The hazard:
data class Range(val start: Int, val end: Int)      // v1
val (s, e) = range
data class Range(val end: Int, val start: Int)      // v2 refactor: compiles, swaps silently
  • Kotlin has been working on name-based destructuring as an alternative. Check the current "What's new" for its status in your Kotlin 2.x version, and don't assume it's stable.
  • Cost: no allocation for data classes. For Pair/Triple the cost is the object itself.
  • Adding a property in the middle of a public data class changes componentN and copy signatures. That's a binary-incompatible change for library consumers, which is one reason library authors avoid public data classes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class User(val id: Long, val name: String, val email: String)

fun render(u: User) {
    val (id, name) = u            // component1(), component2()
    val (_, _, email) = u         // only component3() called
    println("$id $name $email")
}

class Size(val w: Int, val h: Int) {
    operator fun component1() = w
    operator fun component2() = h
}
val (w, h) = Size(10, 20)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Destructuring wide domain objects with same-typed fields (String id/name/email). Positional bugs won't be caught.
  • Confusing { (a, b) -> } with { a, b -> } in lambdas.
  • Assuming destructuring matches variable names to property names. It doesn't: val (name, id) = user gives name = id.
  • Exposing a public data class in an SDK and then appending or reordering properties, which breaks consumers' binaries.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can I destructure a non-data class? → Yes, if it declares operator fun componentN(), either as members or extensions.
  2. How many components are generated? → One per primary-ctor property. There's no artificial cap, unlike the stdlib's 5-component List destructuring extensions.
  3. Why do some style guides ban destructuring of domain models? → It's positional coupling with no compiler protection. They allow it only for Pair and map entries, where position is the semantics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer knows the syntax. The senior answer explains componentN lowering, the silent-swap refactor hazard, the binary compatibility cost of public data classes, and team guidelines on where destructuring is allowed.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team swapped lat/lng order in a LatLng-like data class during a cleanup. A val (lat, lng) = pos in the map renderer put markers in the ocean for one release.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't a data class be open? What can a data class inherit from, and what happens to the generated members when it does?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It probes whether you understand that the language restriction exists to protect the equals contract. It's also the basis of modeling sealed state hierarchies correctly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A data class is implicitly final and can't be open, abstract, sealed or inner. A subclass adding fields would break equals symmetry and make copy() return the wrong type. A data class can extend an open or abstract class and implement interfaces. That's the standard sealed interface UiState + data class Success(...) : UiState pattern. If the parent has final equals/hashCode/toString, the data class uses the parent's versions. If the parent declares open properties, the data class can override them in its constructor.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Why it's final:

  • copy() is fun copy(...): Self. A subclass Sub : Data would inherit a copy() returning Data, losing Sub's fields.
  • Generated equals uses other !is Data. A subclass with extra state would be equal to the parent but not vice versa, which is the symmetry break from Q038.

What's allowed:

Supertype member Effect on generated code
abstract val x / open val x data class override val x in ctor; included in equals
final override fun equals in parent not generated; parent's used (possibly ignoring child props!)
open equals in parent generated override replaces it
final fun componentN with incompatible type compile error
parent ctor properties not redeclared NOT part of data class equals

That last row is a real trap:

abstract class Entity(val id: Long)
data class Note(val text: String, val ownerId: Long) : Entity(ownerId) // id not in equals unless redeclared

The usual recommended shape: put the hierarchy root in a sealed interface (or an abstract class with no state), with data classes or data objects as leaves. Keep shared state in each leaf's constructor, or in a wrapper, rather than in a stateful base class. The sealed vs enum trade-off is covered in chunk K2b.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface Shape { val area: Double }

data class Circle(val r: Double) : Shape {
    override val area get() = Math.PI * r * r // body getter, not part of equals - fine, it's derived
}
data class Rect(val w: Double, val h: Double) : Shape {
    override val area get() = w * h
}

abstract class Base(open val id: String)
data class Item(override val id: String, val title: String) : Base(id) // id included in equals

// data class Sub(val x: Int) : Item("a", "b")   // error: Item is final

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a stateful base class (BaseModel(id, createdAt)) for data classes. Base fields are excluded from equality and copy() can't change them.
  • Writing final override fun equals in a shared base "for logging". It silently disables value equality in every child.
  • Using the all-open compiler plugin (Spring/JPA style) on data classes. It makes them open, so the guarantees disappear. That plugin belongs to chunk K8.
  • Expecting copy() to exist on the interface type. It doesn't, because each leaf has its own signature.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a data class implement Comparable? → Yes. Keep compareTo consistent with equals or TreeSet will dedupe differently from HashSet.
  2. Can a data class be sealed? → No. A sealed parent with data class children is the idiom.
  3. How do you share a copy-like operation across sealed leaves? → An abstract function on the sealed type (fun withLoading(): UiState) implemented in each leaf with its own copy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "data classes are final". The senior answer explains why (copy return type, equals symmetry), lists exactly which parent members suppress generation, flags the "base ctor field not in equals" trap, and recommends stateless sealed roots.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A BaseMessage(id, timestamp) parent with data class children made two different messages with the same text compare equal. DiffUtil merged rows in the chat list.

questions.promptHtml: What can a Kotlin enum class contain? Show constructor properties, per-constant bodies and interface implementation. What does each compile to?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's a fundamentals check, and it sets up follow-ups on allocation, R8 and when an enum should be a sealed type instead.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An enum is a class with a fixed set of instances created once in its static initializer. It can have constructor properties, methods, abstract members that each constant implements in its own body, and it can implement interfaces. Every constant gets name and ordinal. The class gets valueOf(String), values() and, since Kotlin 1.9, entries. A constant with a body compiles to an anonymous subclass. That affects javaClass, so use declaringJavaClass instead.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Bytecode: final class Color extends java.lang.Enum<Color>. It has a public static final Color RED, a private $VALUES array, and since 1.9-compiled code, an $ENTRIES field. <clinit> constructs every constant in order.
  • If any constant has a body, the enum class becomes abstract-ish and the constant is an instance of a synthetic subclass like Color$RED. Then RED.javaClass != Color::class.java. Use RED.declaringJavaClass (Kotlin 1.7+) or Java's declaringClass.
  • valueOf("PURPLE") throws IllegalArgumentException. There's no null-returning variant built in, so use entries.firstOrNull { it.name == s }.
  • ordinal is the declaration position. It isn't stable across reordering, so never persist it (Q051).
  • Enums are Comparable by ordinal, and Serializable through java.lang.Enum. Java serialization of enums is by name and always yields the canonical instance, unlike object (Q055).
  • Android cost: each constant is an object plus static init. Modern R8 can "unbox" simple enums to ints in release builds. Whether a given enum qualifies depends on usage (reflection, valueOf, bodies, being used as a generic type argument) and on the R8 version. The old "never use enums on Android" advice dates from Dalvik and no longer applies.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface Pricing { fun price(base: Int): Int }

enum class Tier(val label: String) : Pricing {
    FREE("Free") {
        override fun price(base: Int) = 0
    },
    PRO("Pro") {
        override fun price(base: Int) = base
    },
    TEAM("Team") {
        override fun price(base: Int) = base * 5
        override fun badge() = "★"
    };                                   // semicolon required before members

    open fun badge(): String = ""

    companion object {
        fun fromLabel(l: String): Tier? = entries.firstOrNull { it.label == l }
    }
}

fun main() {
    println(Tier.TEAM.price(10))                       // 50
    println(Tier.PRO.javaClass == Tier::class.java)    // false - anonymous subclass
    println(Tier.PRO.declaringJavaClass == Tier::class.java) // true
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the ; after the last constant when the enum has members.
  • Using valueOf on server strings without handling unknown values. It throws in production when the backend adds a value.
  • Comparing javaClass for enums with bodies, or using it in reflection-based serializers.
  • Putting mutable state in enum constants. It's global, shared and survives across tests.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can enums have abstract properties? → Yes, each constant must override them in its body, or declare them through the constructor.
  2. Can an enum extend a class? → No, it already extends java.lang.Enum. It can implement interfaces.
  3. When does enum <clinit> run, and can it fail? → On first use of the enum class. An exception there causes ExceptionInInitializerError and then NoClassDefFoundError, the same mechanics as object (Q052).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer shows a property and a when. The senior answer knows constants with bodies become subclasses (declaringJavaClass), that valueOf throws, that ordinal is unstable, and the modern R8 unboxing reality instead of the outdated "avoid enums" advice.
